summary.text: Zosimas and Sabbatius are remembered together as fathers of Solovki. Their lives describe different stages of the island’s monastic foundation; Herman links the earlier solitude of Sabbatius with the later community led by Zosimas.

blocks.text: Sabbatius receives monastic formation at Saint Cyril’s monastery and later Valaam. Seeking greater solitude, he travels toward the White Sea and meets Herman. Together they cross to Solovki and establish cells near Sekirna hill.
blocks.reason: Necessary concise account of the named modern ecclesiastical life; permission for full reproduction has not been established. Traditional events and miracle narratives remain attributed to that publication.

blocks.text: After his parents’ death, Zosimas distributes his possessions and becomes a monk. Herman tells him of the island where he had lived with Sabbatius. Around 1436 they cross to Solovki, cultivate the land, and begin the later community.

blocks.text: The OCA describes Zosimas enduring an isolated winter and later receiving brethren. A wooden Transfiguration church is built. After outside abbots cannot endure the conditions, the community chooses him. He introduces common life and seeks protection from Novgorod’s powerful landowners.

blocks.text: Sabbatius’s earlier account emphasizes humility and the desire to avoid praise. Its sea journeys and island solitude precede the large monastery known from later history. The two men are therefore not collapsed into one simultaneous founding episode.
blocks.reason: Necessary concise account of the named modern ecclesiastical life; permission for full reproduction has not been established. Traditional events and miracle narratives remain attributed to that publication.

blocks.text: Sensing death near, Sabbatius returns to the mainland to receive Communion from Nathanael. He dies peacefully in a cell near the Vyg River on September 27, 1435; Nathanael and a merchant bury him.
blocks.reason: Necessary concise account of the named modern ecclesiastical life; permission for full reproduction has not been established. Traditional events and miracle narratives remain attributed to that publication.

blocks.text: Zosimas prepares his own grave and reposes on April 17, 1478. Neither selected account reports an execution. Their relics are later translated together in 1566.

blocks.text: The later translation of Sabbatius’s relics to the island and joint veneration connect the two stages of Solovki’s history. The lives preserve prayers for sailors, healings, and other miracle traditions as ecclesiastical testimony.

blocks.text: Mouravieff’s church history later names Sabbatius and the Solovki fathers among saints whose veneration was confirmed in the age of Metropolitan Macarius. That passage belongs to a discussion of councils, collected saints’ lives, and the growing commemoration of local holy people throughout Russia. It supplies a later reception context rather than a fresh eyewitness account of the fifteenth-century island foundation. The source’s old transliterations and the damaged line breaks of its scanned edition are left to the retained evidence instead of being silently reconstructed as a quotation.

blocks.text: Sabbatius’s account follows his earlier communities before the island, then his return to the mainland at the end. It names Nathanael and the merchant John at his burial. Keeping those witnesses and places distinct helps separate his life from Zosimas’s later abbacy.
